front: OIL RIG?
back: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain.

front: Oxidising agent vs reducing agent?
back: Oxidising agent is reduced (gains e⁻); reducing agent is oxidised (loses e⁻).

front: Balancing half-equations in acid?
back: Atoms → O with H₂O → H with H⁺ → charge with e⁻.

front: Where do oxidation and reduction happen?
back: Oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode — in every cell.

front: Voltaic vs electrolytic cell?
back: Voltaic: spontaneous, chemical → electrical, anode −. Electrolytic: non-spontaneous, electrical → chemical, anode +.

front: Oxidation products of alcohols?
back: 1°: aldehyde (distil) → acid (reflux). 2°: ketone. 3°: none. Orange → green.

front: Reducing carbonyls and acids?
back: NaBH₄/LiAlH₄: aldehyde → 1° alcohol, ketone → 2° alcohol; LiAlH₄ for acids.

front: (HL) Standard hydrogen electrode?
back: H₂ (100 kPa) on Pt in 1 mol dm⁻³ H⁺ at 298 K; E⦵ = 0.00 V.

front: (HL) E⦵cell and spontaneity?
back: E⦵cathode − E⦵anode; positive → spontaneous.

front: (HL) ΔG⦵ from E⦵cell?
back: ΔG⦵ = −nFE⦵cell, F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹.

front: (HL) Aqueous electrolysis rules?
back: Cathode: Cu/Ag deposited, else H₂. Anode: conc. halide → halogen, else O₂.

front: Oxidation and reduction in terms of oxidation state?
back: Oxidation: increase in oxidation state. Reduction: decrease. A redox reaction contains both.

front: Reduction half-equation for MnO₄⁻ in acid?
back: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O (purple → colourless; Mn +7 → +2).

front: Reduction half-equation for Cr₂O₇²⁻ in acid?
back: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O (orange → green; Cr +6 → +3).

front: Combining half-equations into an overall equation?
back: Multiply so electrons lost = electrons gained, add, then cancel electrons and species on both sides (H⁺, H₂O).

front: Using the activity series in redox?
back: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal ion from solution: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu (Zn is the reducing agent).

front: Which metals react with dilute acids to give H₂?
back: Metals above H in the activity series: Mg + 2H⁺ → Mg²⁺ + H₂. Cu, Ag, Au do not.

front: Role of the salt bridge?
back: Completes the circuit and maintains electrical neutrality by letting ions (e.g. K⁺, NO₃⁻) move between half-cells; no electrons flow through it.

front: Direction of electron flow in a Zn/Cu voltaic cell?
back: From the Zn anode (−, oxidised) through the external wire to the Cu cathode (+); cations in the salt bridge move towards the cathode.

front: Cell notation for the Daniell cell?
back: Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(aq) ‖ Cu²⁺(aq) | Cu(s) — anode on the left, ‖ is the salt bridge.

front: Primary vs secondary cells?
back: Primary: non-rechargeable (reaction irreversible), e.g. zinc–carbon. Secondary: rechargeable by reversing the reaction with external current, e.g. lithium-ion, lead–acid.

front: Electrolysis of molten NaCl: products and half-equations?
back: Cathode (−): Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na(l). Anode (+): 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂(g) + 2e⁻.

front: Do electrons flow through the electrolyte?
back: No. Electrons flow in the external circuit; ions carry charge through the electrolyte.

front: Distillation vs reflux in oxidising ethanol?
back: Distil immediately: ethanal (aldehyde) escapes before further oxidation. Heat under reflux with excess oxidant: ethanoic acid.

front: Reduction of alkenes by hydrogen?
back: C=C + H₂ → C–C with Ni catalyst at ~150 °C (or Pt/Pd); e.g. ethene → ethane; used to harden vegetable oils.

front: (HL) What does a more positive E⦵ mean?
back: The oxidised form is a stronger oxidising agent (more easily reduced). The most negative E⦵ → strongest reducing agent (e.g. Li).

front: (HL) E⦵cell for Zn/Cu cell (E⦵ Zn²⁺/Zn = −0.76 V, Cu²⁺/Cu = +0.34 V)?
back: +0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V; spontaneous, Cu²⁺ reduced.

front: (HL) Do you multiply E⦵ when a half-equation is doubled?
back: No. E⦵ is an intensive property — independent of stoichiometric coefficients (unlike ΔG⦵).

front: (HL) ΔG⦵ for the Zn/Cu cell (E⦵cell = 1.10 V)?
(HL) Products of electrolysing concentrated NaCl(aq) (inert electrodes)?
back: Cathode: H₂ (2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻). Anode: Cl₂ (2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻). NaOH left in solution.

front: (HL) Anode product for dilute NaCl(aq) and why?
back: O₂: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻; with dilute Cl⁻, water is oxidised preferentially.

front: (HL) Setup for copper electroplating?
back: Object to be plated is the cathode, pure Cu is the anode, electrolyte contains Cu²⁺(aq). Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu at cathode; Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ at anode, so [Cu²⁺] stays constant.

front: (HL) Electrolysis of CuSO₄(aq) with inert electrodes: observations?
back: Cathode: copper deposits (pink). Anode: O₂ bubbles. Blue colour fades and solution becomes acidic (H⁺ forms).
